\chapter{Morning}
\label{ch:ka-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} in Kannada using the language's own native word for it.}

Say \kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}, trace it to beḷagu (\textquotedblleft{}to dawn\textquotedblright{}) and beḷaku (\textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{}), and contrast it with the Sanskrit dina, rātri and madhyāhna around it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}]{\kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ} (beḷagge) — the one time-word that's genuinely Kannada's own}

\label{lesson:KA-C26-belagge}



\begin{quote}
Every everyday time-word you've met in Kannada so far — day, night, noon, midnight — has been Sanskrit, borrowed whole. This one breaks that pattern completely.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}} (\textbf{beḷagge}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{} — is \textbf{native Dravidian}, built on \textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳಗು}} (\emph{beḷagu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to shine, to become bright, to dawn}\textquotedblright{}) and the related noun \textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳಕು}} (\emph{beḷaku}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{light}\textquotedblright{}). Morning is, quite literally, \textquotedblleft{}the shining,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the dawning\textquotedblright{} — a transparent, homegrown metaphor, no borrowed vocabulary anywhere in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's what makes this lesson different from every other Kannada time-word lesson so far: \textbf{\kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{dina}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{\kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ}} (\emph{ratri}, \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} (\emph{madhyāhna}, \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{}) are all genuine \textbf{Sanskrit tatsama} borrowings, taken whole, doing the plain everyday job in Kannada. \textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}} breaks that streak — it's the one everyday time-word in this set that's actually \textbf{Kannada's own}, not a loan from anywhere. If you'd only met \emph{dina}, \emph{ratri}, and \emph{madhyāhna}, you might start to assume every Kannada time-word is Sanskrit underneath. This one is the honest counter-example — though, matching the pattern already seen with \emph{hagalu} and \emph{iruḷu} (Chapters 23–24), a native compound for \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} does technically exist too: \textbf{\kn{ನಡುಹಗಲು}} (\emph{naḍuhagalu}, \textquotedblleft{}middle-of-daytime,\textquotedblright{} built from \emph{naḍu}, \textquotedblleft{}middle,\textquotedblright{} the same everyday word already met, plus \emph{hagalu}). It just lost the everyday job to \emph{madhyāhna}, the same way \emph{hagalu} and \emph{iruḷu} were pushed into narrower, or archaic, roles by their own Sanskrit competitors.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}beḷagge\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} native Dravidian
  \item the root — beḷagu, \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to dawn,\textquotedblright{} and beḷaku, \textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — dina, ratri, madhyāhna are all Sanskrit; beḷagge is genuinely Kannada's own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What native root does \kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ} come from, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳಗು}/\kn{ಬೆಳಕು}} — \textquotedblleft{}to shine/dawn\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}light.\textquotedblright{}) Is \kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ} a Sanskrit tatsama, like dina, ratri, and madhyāhna? (\textbf{No} — genuinely native Dravidian, the odd one out among Kannada's everyday time-words.)
\end{tcolorbox}
